analytic.title: An Open Real-Time Environment for Parallel and Distributed Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Most computer-based systems have hard real-time constraints. Schedulers in complex systems must be designed to manage a set of applications developed and deployed independently. In this paper, we study an open real-time environment architecture for distributed systems where r eal-time applications may run concurrently with non-real-time applications. The architecture uses a two-level scheduling scheme. Each application is assigned a sporadic server to schedule the processes in the application. Allsporadic servers are then scheduled by a system-wide xed priority scheduler. Using the proposed open environment architecture, all hard real-time applications are guaranteed to have their reserved CPU utilization in order to meet all their deadlines. The guarantee is independent of the behaviors of all other applications in the same system. We present the schedulability analysis methods on systems with or without shared memory.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In the past decades, there is an increasing demand for distributed systems with real-time or response-time requirements. Several complex real-time applications may be developed independently and then run on a distributed computing system concurrently with some non-real-time applications. For example, an automated factory control system may have several hard realtime sensor monitoring applications, several soft realtime multimedia processing applications, as well as Supported for the rst author in part by Pan-Wen-Yuan Foundation and a research grant from the ROC National Science Council under Grant NSC87-2213-E-194-002. The research was also supported in part by UC MICRO 99-073 and 99-074, Raytheon and GeoSpatial Technologies, and by US NSF CCR-9901697.

non-real-time MIS and desk top applications running concurrently in a distributed computing environment. Although each hard real-time application may have been veri ed to meet its deadlines when running by itself, its performance may not be as predictable when it is running concurrently with a random or dynamic set of other applications. We need a rigorous and sound methodology to compose complex real-time systems from independently designed real-time applications.

The idea of open real-time environment was rst proposed by Liu,et al. 4, 5 to solve the real-time composability problem. In an open real-time environment, real-time and non-real-time applications are allowed to join and leave the system dynamically. However, the schedulability of each real-time application must be guaranteed independent of any other applications in the system. In 4, 5 , a two-level hierarchical scheduling scheme following the idea of the GPS scheduling scheme 18 is proposed to provide a fair sharing of computing budget among applications running on the same processor. Applications are scheduled for execution by a constant utilization server CUS 4, 5 . Each CUS server has its reserved CPU budget and is scheduled by an earliest-deadline-rst EDF scheduler 12 in the kernel. Using the reserved computing budget for the servers, the schedulability for real-time applications with or without shared global resources can be guaranteed 5 .

The open environment proposed in 4, 5 relies on the EDF scheduler in the kernel. Since many existing operating systems support only xed-priority s c heduling, it is desirable to implement the open environment architecture using xed-priority s c hedulers as well. Kuo and Li 10 t h us extend the open environment architecture to systems with a xed-priority kernel scheduler. In their proposed scheme, each real-time or non-real-time application is scheduled for execution by a sporadic server 14 . All sporadic servers are then scheduled by a rate monotonic 12 xed priority k ernel scheduler with their reserved CPU capacities. Schedulability tests for applications with or without shared resources have also been investigated 10 .

This paper extends the xed-priority o p e n e n vironment scheme in 10 from a single processor system to parallel and distributed computing systems. Using the same base architecture as in 10 , we propose a global scheduler for all processors. All applications are submitted to a global admission controller before their deployment. If admitted, a sporadic server will be created to schedule processes in the application. The global scheduler will decide when and which processor to execute the sporadic server and, in turn, the application. By extending the schedulability analysis from single-processor systems to multi-processor systems, we can guarantee that all admitted real-time processes can meet their deadlines. With the proposed open real-time environment, we h a ve a feasible solution to the di cult composability problem of parallel and distributed realtime computing systems. Our work thus provides a new direction and methodology on building distributed real-time systems.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the base architecture of a singleprocessor open real-time environment. We extend the architecture to parallel and distributed systems in Section 3. The resource synchronization issue for applications with shared resources is investigated in Section 4. The paper is concluded in Section 5.

div.head: The Open Real-Time Environment Architecture
div.p: Rate-driven scheduling has been an active research topic in the past decade. Researchers have proposed various rate-driven scheduling algorithms for periodic and sporadic processes based on the notion of General Processor Sharing GPS 1, 9, 16, 1 8 . GPS is a scheduling algorithm based on the concept of the reservation ratio of processor computation time. Suppose a GPS server executes at a xed rate r which is usually one, and each process i has a reservation ratio i which is a positive real number. Each process i is guaranteed to be served at a rate of g i = i P j j r independent of the actual workloads of other processes.

In other words, the guaranteed CPU service rate g i for i will not be a ected by the actual behavior of any j , i 6 = j. The enforcement of the guaranteed CPU service rate for a process must rely on an admission control mechanism to manage the total workload of a system 15 . The GPS-based scheduling allows any ready process to use any left-over CPU time not used by any other admitted process in the system. Therefore, the system will not be left idle as long as there are processes waiting to be executed. On the other hand, with the guaranteed CPU service rate, a real-time process can meet all its deadlines as long as its actual workload does not exceed its reserved rate.

Using the guaranteed CPU sharing scheme similar to GPS, Liu et Figure 1 shows the open system architecture supported by the two-level hierarchical scheme. In this architecture, the operating system uses a xed-priority scheduler. If the system has only one processor, then its CPU capacity is one. If the system consists of M processors, then its capacity i s M. Note that a multiprocessor system can be either loosely or tightly coupled. We will consider both types of systems in this paper.

There are real-time and non-real-time applications executing in an open environment. The system has an admission controller which decides if a new real-time application can be feasibly scheduled. Each application A i is scheduled by a sporadic server S i 14 with a CPU budget c i and a period p i . Each sporadic server maintains a ready queue which contains all ready processes from the application. Each sporadic server may use a di erent scheduling algorithm , i , such as EDF or RM, to schedule processes in the ready queue of S i . For example, Figure 1 shows that server S 0 uses a time sharing algorithm to schedule processes in application A 0 , and S 1 uses the RM scheduling for A 1 .

The scheduler used in the operating system is called the kernel scheduler KS. KS manages all sporadic servers in the system. Note that when a distributed system is considered, KS is the scheduler on the master node i.e. a master slave architecture is considered for a distributed real-time system in this paper. KS replenishes the budget of each sporadic server according to the sporadic server algorithm. A sporadic server is ready if its ready queue is not empty. KS schedules all ready sporadic servers according to a xed-priority scheduling algorithm. Since the rate monotonic RM scheduling algorithm is an optimal xed-priority s c heduling algorithm, we use RM as the scheduling algorithm for KS in this paper. Processes under a scheduled sporadic server may execute until the budget of the sporadic server runs out, or a higherpriority sporadic server becomes ready. On the other hand, processes under a sporadic server are executed in the order de ned by the scheduling algorithm , i selected for the server S i .
The operations of the kernel scheduler are summarized below.

div.head: Initiation of an application A i :
div.p: Create a sporadic server S i with a CPU budget c i and a period p i for a new application A i if A i passes the admission control.

div.head: Scheduling of sporadic servers:
div.p: The kernel scheduler schedules the ready sporadic server with the highest priority.

div.head: Maintenance of each sporadic server S i :
div.p: The budget replenishment mechanism is conducted according to the sporadic server algorithm de ned in 14 discussed next.

div.head: Interaction between processes and servers:
div.p: Each sporadic server S i schedules processes according to algorithm , i .
The scheduled process of each server S i executes using only the budget of S i .

div.head: Completion of an application:
div.p: Remove the corresponding sporadic server.

div.head: Scheduling Hierarchy and Admission Control 2.2.1 Sporadic Servers
div.p: Sporadic servers 14 are originally proposed for servicing sporadic process requests. Sporadic requests assigned to a sporadic server can use the CPU budget of the server for execution. Each sporadic server is associated with a CPU budget c i and a period p i . Suppose that the system is scheduled by a xed-priority s c heduler. Let P s denote the priority o f the process which is executing. A priority level P i is active if P s P i .
A priority level is idle if it is not active. The budget replenishment mechanism of a sporadic server in a uniprocessor system is summarized as follows.
Let RT i denote the replenishment time for a sporadic server with priority P i and period p i .
The replenishment time RT i of server S i is set as follows:
If S i has a non-zero remaining CPU budget, and P i becomes active at time t, then RT i = t + p i .
If the CPU budget of S i is exhausted, and the CPU budget of S i was last replenished at time t, then RT i = t + p i .
The replenishment amount is equal to the amount of server execution time consumed when P i becomes idle before RT i , or when the CPU budget of S i becomes zero.

It has been shown 14 that the schedulability analysis of sporadic servers is equivalent to that of periodic processes with the same p i and c i . The following example illustrates the basic idea of a sporadic server.
Example 1 Sporadic Server:

Let a system consist of a periodic process 1 and a sporadic server S executing in a uniprocessor environment, where the period and the CPU requirement o f 1 are 6 and 3, respectively. The CPU budget and the period of S are 1 and 4, respectively. The sporadic server is used to service sporadic requests. Suppose that the OS scheduler adopts RM scheduling. The priority o f S is higher than the priority o f 1 .

Figure 2 shows the executions of 1 and S. At time 0, only 1 is ready and is scheduled to execute. The priority level of the sporadic server is idle. At time 1, the rst sporadic request arrives, and one unit of CPU time is required to process the request. S is scheduled to execute at time 1 because S has a higher priority than 1 . Since the priority level of S becomes active Figure 2: Executions of a sporadic server at time 1, the replenishment time RT is set as 5 that is equal to the current time t plus the period of S. At time 2, the CPU budget of S is exhausted, and the rst sporadic request is ful lled. The replenishment amount is set as 1. Since the priority level of S is idle again, 1 resumes its execution and nishes at time 4. At time 5, the CPU budget of S is replenished. When the second sporadic request arrives at time 6, S is executed again to service the request. 2

div.head: Scheduling Sporadic Servers and Admission Control
div.p: Since the rate monotonic RM scheduling algorithm is an optimal xed-priority s c heduling algorithm, RM is used as the kernel scheduler in our open system architecture. The priorities of servers are inversely proportional to their periods. The server with the smallest period has the highest priority in the system. When two servers have the same period, their priority order is determined arbitrarily. When a sporadic server is used to execute a nonreal-time application, the period and the CPU budget of the server can be set arbitrarily. However, the period length should be reasonably small to make the application responsive to user inputs. The amount o f t h e CPU budget determines the amount of the CPU capacity reserved for the non-real-time application. When a sporadic server is used to execute a real-time application, the period of the server must be no larger than d i =2 + d ci c e for any process i with CPU requirement c i and relative deadline d i in the real-time application, where c is the CPU budget of the server. This is because the sporadic server is only guaranteed to receive c units of CPU cycles within every p units of time, as shown in Figure 3.

In order to better utilize the CPU cycles, let the periods of all sporadic servers in the system be harmonically related, i.e., they are all multiples of some base periods. Moreover, if a period of a server can not divide the period of another server, then the latter must be able to divide the former. A periodic process set that is schedulable with a periodic process i is also schedulable if i is replaced with a sporadic server with the same period and CPU budget. The schedulability analysis of sporadic servers is thus equivalent to that of periodic processes. Moreover, Kuo and Mok 8 h a ve shown that the achievable utilization factor of any periodic process set with periods being harmonically related is 100. The achievable utilization factor of a collection of sporadic servers with periods being harmonically related is thus 100. Let the utilization factor of a server is the ratio of its CPU budget and period. The admission control mechanism in a uniprocessor environment is as follows:

Let U be the sum of utilization factors of all sporadic servers currently in the system. A new application A i with a sporadic server S i is admitted to the system if U +U i 100, where U i is the utilization factor of S i .
When there are more than one processors, the total utilization factor will be larger than one. This will be discussed in more details in the next section.
3 Open Environment for Parallel and Distributed Systems

In the last section, we present the two-level hierarchical scheme for scheduling independently developed real-time and non-real-time applications. The underlying system can be a uniprocessor system, a loosely or tightly coupled multiprocessor system.

div.head: Parallel System Model
div.p: The proposed parallel system architecture is an extension from the single processor open environment scheme in 10 . Using the same base architecture as in 10 , we use a global scheduler for all processors in a parallel system. All applications are submitted to a global admission controller before their deployment. If admitted, a sporadic server will be created to schedule processes in the application. The global scheduler will decide when and which processor to execute a sporadic server, and, in turn, processes of the application.

In a tightly-coupled multiprocessor system, we assume that all processors can access a global shared memory. The kernel scheduler can determine the scheduling of any process on any processor at any time. We also assume the cost for process migration from one processor to another is negligible. This is in contrast to a loosely-coupled multiprocessor system when the system has many distributed processors without any global memory. The cost of migrating any process across processors, i.e., computing nodes, is signicant in a loosely-coupled system. Therefore, the kernel scheduler proposed in this paper does not allow process migrations in a loosely-coupled system. We will consider the system model that allows process migrations in our future work. Each application and thus the sporadic server created for it will be assigned a computing node at the admission control process and will be executed on that node until it terminates. Although this may not be the most e cient w ay of utilizing a parallel system, the assumption makes our scheduling decision much easier. Another assumption is that no process with parallel processing threads will be considered in our current study.

Let a real-time application A i consist of n independent periodic processes 1 ; 2 ; ; n , where each process j has a CPU requirement c j and a period p j , and the relative deadline d j of each process j be equal to its period p j . Suppose that a sporadic server S i with a CPU budget C and a period P is used to execute application A i , and the reserved capacity o f A i is C P .

We assume the period P of the server be the greatest common divisor GCD or a divisor of the GCD of all process periods in the application, and the initial phase of each process occurs at a time point which i s a multiple of P.

Since each application A i which passes the admission control described later is guaranteed to receive a t least C units of CPU cycles within every P time units because of the sporadic server mechanism, processes in A i will only compete the reserved CPU budget among themselves. The schedulability analysis of each application can be done independently of other applications in the system. In this section, we rst derive a su cient condition for a real-time application which adopts the rate monotonic RM scheduling algorithm and a sucient and necessary condition for those which adopt the earliest deadline rst EDF scheduling algorithm 12 .

We propose the admission control mechanism for parallel and distributed systems. We will show that servers that are harmonically related can fully utilize all of the processors in a parallel system. The admission control problem of new applications in a distributed system is, however, a bin packing problem.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: We will now extend the uniprocessor schedulability tests proposed in 10 to multiprocessor systems. Let a parallel system consist of M processors. The system computing capacity i s t h us equal to M. Note that A i only reserves C M P of the entire system CPU capacity.

Suppose that each sporadic server S i executes on at most one processor at any time. In other words, even if there are more than one ready processes in application A i , and there is more than one idle CPU, only one ready process will be dispatched for execution. We assume processes do not share any resource other than CPU in this section. We will consider non-preemptable resource synchronization later in this paper.

div.p: Let a real-time application A i be serviced by sporadic server S i which uses the EDF scheduling algorithm. The CPU requirement c j of each process j is measured in terms of the system with a speed equal to one where one processor is deployed.

A priority level is idle if it is not active. When a priority level is idle, only servers with lower priorities can be executing, and or some processors are idle.

Theorem 3 can be proved in a way similar to the corresponding theorem for uniprocessor systems in 10 .

div.head: Admission Control
div.p: We n o w i n vestigate the admission control for an open environment in a parallel system with M processors. We rst show that servers which are harmonically related i.e. their periods are harmonic numbers can fully utilize all processors in a parallel system. Theorem 4 8 In a uniprocessor system, the least upper bound of the utilization factor for any process set in which the periods are selected f r om K harmonic chains is at least K2 1 K , 1. Corollary 1 In a uniprocessor system, the least upper bound of the utilization factor for any process set in which the periods are selected f r om one harmonic chain is 100. Theorem 5 In an M-processor parallel system, the least upper bound of the utilization factor for any process set in which the periods are selected f r om one harmonic chain is M.

Corollary 1 follows directly from Theorem 4 with K = 1, and Theorem 5 follows directly from Corollary 1 because the process migration cost among processors is negligible, and all processors are the same.
Since all server periods are harmonically related, the M processors in a parallel system can be fully utilized.
Let a new real-time or non-real-time application with a utilization factor equals to U i arrive at a parallel system with M processors. We can de ne the admission control mechanism as follows:

Let U be the sum of utilization factors of all sporadic servers in the system. A new application A i with a sporadic server S i is admitted to the system if U +U i M, where U i is the utilization factor of S i , and the period o f S i is harmonically related to all other periods.

div.head: Distributed Systems with Loosely-Coupled Processors
div.p: For distributed systems with loosely-coupled processors, the process migration cost across computing nodes is signi cant. We therefore assume that each application is executed on only one processor. We also assume that any application considered in this paper will require no more than one CPU at a time. Let a distributed system consist of M identical computing nodes. Since each application executes on only one computing node, the system scheduler must assign the sporadic server for an application to a computing node if the application passes the admission control. After that, the scheduling issue for the sporadic server will be the same as in the uniprocessor case.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis RM Server Scheduler:
div.p: Suppose server S i uses the RM scheduling algorithm.

Since each sporadic server executes on a computing node and will not migrate across computing nodes, theorems for achievable utilization factor remain similar. Theorem 6 The achievable utilization factor of the RM scheduler of server S i in a distributed system is U = C P n2 1=n , 1.

Theorem 6 can be proved in the same way as Theorem 2 since each sporadic server executes only on one computing node. EDF Server Scheduler: Let P j s denote the priority of the sporadic server which is executing on the j th computing node in a distributed system. A priority level P i is active on the j th computing node if P j s P i . A priority level is idle on the j th computing node if it is not active. Note that different computing servers service di erent applications and may h a ve di erent P j s .

Lemma 1 When EDF is used to schedule processes in application A i in a distributed system, there i s n o i d l e time for server S i prior to an over ow. Theorem 7 For a set of n periodic processes serviced by a sporadic server S i with a period P and a CPU budget C in a distributed system, EDF is feasible if and only if P cj pj C P . Lemma 1 and Theorem 7 can be proved in a way similar to the corresponding Lemma for uniprocessor systems in 10 and Theorem 3, respectively, since each sporadic server stays at one computing node.

div.head: Admission Control
div.p: To guarantee that all real-time applications can meet their deadlines, an open environment m ust conduct admission control before any real-time application is deployed in the distributed system. Since no sporadic server, i.e., application, may migrate across computing nodes, and each sporadic server executes on one processor, the admission control problem of new applications is, in fact, a bin packing problem.

Let a new real-time or non-real-time application with utilization factor equal to U i arrive at a distributed system with M computing nodes, and the sum of utilization factors of all admitted sporadic servers on each computing node Node j be U S j . Since all server periods are harmonically related, the processor of each computing node in a distributed system can be fully utilized. As long as there exists any computing node Node j such that U S j + U i 100, the new application can be assigned to that computing node. Note that each computing node is like a bin with a capacity equal to 100, and each application is like an item to be packed in the M bins of the distributed system which has M computing nodes. Our requirement in assigning each sporadic server with a distinct priority level does not invalidate the above s c hedulability test because servers with the same period have consecutive priority levels.

In this paper, due to the space constraint, we only present a general admission control mechanism de ned below. We refer interested readers to previous research results on the bin packing problem. In the worst case, the system may be only 50 utilized if all applications need a utilization slightly more than 50 of any single-CPU utilization.

Let U S j be the sum of utilization factors of all sporadic servers on the j th computing node in the distributed system. A new application A i with a sporadic server S i is admitted to the system and execute on the j th computing node if U S j + U i 100, where U i is the utilization factor of S i .

div.head: Resource Sharing in Open Environment
div.p: The discussion in the last section presents e cient schedulability tests for real-time applications which d o not share any resources in the applications. In this section, we discuss possible protocols to facilitate resource sharing in an open environment.

For real-time systems using the xed-priority scheduling, Sha, Rajkumar, and Lehoczky 17 have proposed the priority ceiling protocol PCP to control the blocking delay due to resources sharing among realtime processes. Using PCP, a process holding a shared resource will inherit the highest priority of all processese waiting to use the resource. The priority ceiling of a resource is the priority of the highest priority process that may use the resource. A process's resource request is blocked if its priority i s no larger than the priority ceiling of any resource which has been grabbed by another process at the time and has not yet been released. Another real-time resource sharing protocol, the stack resource p olicy SRP was proposed by Baker 2 for systems with dynamic priority assignments such as EDF. SRP is based on the same concept of implicit locking.

Suppose that a sporadic server S i with a CPU budget C and a period P is used to execute application A i , and the reserved capacity o f A i is C P . Suppose application A i uses a real-time resource synchronization algorithm, such as PCP or SRP. Since each server is guaranteed with the reserved CPU budget in every period, regardless of whether processes serviced by the server share local resources, the schedulability tests of PCP and SRP can be extended directly from those of RM and EDF. Dut to the space constraint, we present the following theorems without proof, and skip the admission control mechanism in this paper.

Theorem 9 Processes in application A i which adopts SRP are schedulable in a parallel or distributed system if 8 k=1;;n k; P k i=1 ci pi + b k p k C P , where b k is the execution time of the longest critical section of any process whose relative deadline, i.e., period, is less than that of k , and C and P are the CPU budget and the period o f the server for A i , r espectively.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Work
div.p: We h a ve proposed a xed-priority-based open realtime environment architecture for parallel and distributed systems in this paper. An open environment allows real-time and non-real-time applications to be integrated and executed concurrently in the same system. The proposed architecture is an extension from the single processor open environment scheme in 10 to parallel and distributed systems. Using the same base architecture as in 10 , we may feasibly schedule applications which h a ve prcesses sharing resources. By extending the schedulability analysis from singleprocessor systems to multi-processor systems, we can guarantee that all admitted real-time processes can meet their deadlines.

The proposed open environment architecture is an important step toward building distributed real-time systems with many di erent applications. However, many assumptions have been made in this paper about the applications. For example, no process migration is allowed and no parallel threads can be executed by a process. These assumptions make our base model easier to analyze and to understand. To make the open environment more practical, however, we m a y need to relax some of the assumptions. We will continue this research to make the model more general and explore resource sharing across applications in the system.
